rationale: No panel dissent is carried in the packet. The judgment changed, so a complete assessment is returned. Two primary papers entered the ledger since the incumbent and they alter treatments without moving any verdict: Ballyns 2011 (VASO-E022–E030) and Simons, Hong & Simons 2002 (VASO-E031–E032). (1) VASO-C002's statement itself now reads as a prevalence gradient across the endplate zone rather than an exclusive nidus; VASO-E031 records endplate noise at 4 of 11 non-tender endplate-zone sites, so the incumbent's article text ('none in the non-tender sites') and its treatment of C002 as an addressable island are no longer faithful. Verdict stays provisionally_supported; diagnosticity is lowered and the strongest objection becomes that the signature tracks the endplate zone first. (2) VASO-C003's treatment changes for the same reason: neither Hubbard–Berkoff nor McNulty placed a control needle in a matched endplate-zone site, which is now the named weakest point of the 'brain has the knot's address' reading (VASO-R011). (3) VASO-C005's reasoning now rests on a primary blinded-sonographer study rather than second-hand Mazza: strong graded stiffness separation (VASO-E023), a group-level Doppler difference (VASO-E022), a null resistivity index and poor classifier performance (VASO-E024, VASO-E025), and no pain-free controls (VASO-E026). Verdict holds at provisionally_supported; confidence rises. (4) VASO-E027 is entered as weak support for C020 but the ledger's own second reader disputes the direction; I treat it as zero-diagnosticity context because the source names contracture-compression (the conventional account) as a co-equal cause and never mentions smooth-muscle latch. C020 stays unresolved. Selection: six unfeatured observation claims anchored by the new primaries are now featured (VASO-C031–C036), bringing the set to twenty; they are the strongest new instrumented evidence and they cut symmetrically — the stiffness gradient and pulsatility difference support 'something is there', while retrograde flow at 31% of normal sites, the null resistivity index, and endplate noise outside trigger points cut against a discrete vascular marker and an exclusive nidus. Load-bearing set unchanged (C020, C004, C010, C012, C002); weakest links unchanged. Crux order: VASO-R012 (open the unretrieved primaries — Olewnik 2025 in particular would give C011 its first objective imaged record and qualify C004's two-key framing) moves to third, and VASO-R011 (matched endplate-zone control under mental arithmetic) to fourth, because both are cheap and each directly sharpens a featured observation. The article is retold with the Ballyns and Simons detail in the phenomenon and neural-signature sections, the conventional account now states the endplate-zone reading and the authors' own compression alternatives, and the crux list gains the matched-control test. Case verdict remains unresolved as a finding: the decisive experiment is specified, cheap and unrun.
article:
There is a strange gap at the center of musculoskeletal medicine. Anyone with a foam roller and twenty minutes can find [dozens of small, discrete, exquisitely tender points in their own body]{claim=VASO-C001} — most densely around the hips and shoulders, by common report more numerous with each passing decade. Roll across one and it announces itself. Yet open the research literature and you find scientists arguing about what these points are — and, in part, [about whether the “trigger point” is a real, reliably identifiable thing at all]{claim=VASO-C030}.

This case examines a chain of ideas offered to close that gap. It runs from textbook smooth-muscle physiology, through a minority hypothesis about blood and computation, to Tibetan and Indian contemplative anatomy, and it arrives at a proposal with a slogan: a knot is a *state*, not a *scar* — something the body is actively doing and could stop doing, rather than tissue that has been damaged. The lower rungs of the chain are established science. The upper rungs have never been tested. And the one experiment that would decide the central question has never been run.

## A phenomenon without a mechanism

Part of the reason the fight has run so long is structural. Medicine is organized by organ system: orthopedics owns bones, neurology owns nerves, cardiology owns the pipes. Nobody owns muscle tone — the continuous, neurally set background contraction of soft tissue. No specialty means no billing codes, no imaging protocols, no funding lines. The skeptics’ favorite line, “there is no evidence,” is partly circular: there is little evidence in part because nobody has been paid to look.

But the skeptical case deserves its full weight, and it is heavier than proponents usually grant. A systematic review of examination-reliability studies (Lucas and colleagues, 2009) concluded that manual examination for trigger points has not been shown to be reliable or valid — partly because no accepted reference standard exists for what one is — and could not be recommended as an objective diagnostic test. The most pointed peer-reviewed critique (Quintner, Bove and Cohen, 2015) argues that the construct rests on circular reasoning: the lesion has never been demonstrated, examiners disagree, and the clinical phenomena can be explained otherwise. That critique drew a rebuttal, and the exchange rather than either paper is the state of the debate. Even the construct’s defenders concede the core of the complaint: the NIH-affiliated imaging group whose work appears below writes that examination results “can vary depending on the clinician’s training and experience,” and that palpation and pain scores remain the reference standard while being “still subjective measures.” The dispute, then, is not only about mechanism. It reaches the observation base: the reproducibility and even the ontological status of the discrete palpable spot are part of the academic argument. That is why this case grades the first claim above as *provisionally* rather than *well* supported — the shared experience is vast, but the instrumented record behind “discrete” and “palpable” is thinner than it feels under the fingertip. The only population figure the ledger holds is a 1986 clinic-based estimate, quoted second-hand in a 2011 introduction, that myofascial pain affects some 23 million Americans; that is a prevalence for a pain syndrome, not a count of tender points in ordinary people. The essay this case grew from points to fibromyalgia-era community exams using an eighteen-site tender-point protocol, said to find tender points nearly universal with counts tracking distress rather than tissue damage, but the underlying surveys have not been traced in this project, and until they are, the figures carry no weight here.

What survives the critique is a set of instrumented findings, and they deserve to be seen in detail, because they cut both ways. Shah and colleagues (2008) sampled the fluid at active trigger points and found [it more acidic and loaded with mediators of pain and inflammation — bradykinin, substance P, CGRP]{claim=VASO-C005}. The study had about nine volunteers and, as its own title says, the mediators were elevated at sites remote from the points as well as near them. Something is there, and it is chemically angry — but whether what is there is *local* is less settled than it sounds.

The most detailed instrumented look comes from the same NIH lineage. In 2011 Ballyns, Shah and colleagues imaged the upper trapezius of forty-four patients with acute neck pain, 169 sites in all, with the sonographers blinded to which sites the examiner had called active (painful on its own), latent (painful only when pressed), or normal. Vibration sonoelastography — shaking the tissue with a handheld massager and mapping where it fails to move — found [a graded region of stiffness: about 0.57 square centimeters at active points, 0.36 at latent points, and 0.17 at palpably normal sites]{claim=VASO-C033}, and the area separated the three classes well, with an area under the curve of 0.9 for active against normal. Color Doppler found prominent vessels near the points, and [arteries within a centimeter or two of active points showed a pulsatility index — a measure of how sharply flow surges and falls with each heartbeat — of 8.3, against 3.0 near normal sites]{claim=VASO-C031}, with flow running backward between heartbeats in 55 percent of active sites. That is the finding proponents read as the footprint of something clenched upstream.

The same paper contains the qualifiers. [Backward diastolic flow also appeared near 31 percent of palpably normal sites]{claim=VASO-C032}, so the waveform is a gradient across symptomatic muscle rather than a marker of a knot. [The resistivity index — a companion measure of downstream resistance — did not differ at all between active, latent and normal sites]{claim=VASO-C036}, and the pulsatility index varied so widely that it could not classify any individual site; the authors report that the blood-flow measures “did not perform well as classifiers.” There was no pain-free control group: the “normal” sites were simply five centimeters away in a muscle that had a trigger point somewhere else, and the authors say plainly that their flow findings “do not represent the normal variation.” The vessels interrogated were pulsatile arteries or enlarged arterioles typically more than a millimeter across, one to two centimeters from the point — not the microvessels a latch account would need. And the authors list, as candidate causes of the high-resistance flow, muscle contracture compressing the capillary bed, the anatomy of the trapezius apex, inflammatory vasoconstriction, and pressure from the transducer itself. A 2021 systematic review of 33 imaging studies, characterized in this ledger only second-hand, reports that stiffness and blood-flow measures can distinguish active and latent points from healthy tissue, with reproducibility caveats attached. The sum: palpated knots are objectively stiffer, in a graded way, and the local arteries behave somewhat differently — but the vascular signature is partial, and nothing in it says what the stiff tissue is.

Then there is the phenomenology practitioners report, which any candidate mechanism must explain. The obstruction feels like a dull blockage rather than a sharp stretch-pain. Knots accumulate and hold flexibility hostage. And — the strange one — [pressure locates a knot, but release comes with breath: press in, exhale slowly, and something lets go within seconds]{claim=VASO-C004}. Fresh knots yield in a session; old ones take months. This case labels that report for what it is: first-person testimony from the hypothesis’s own proponent, in an essay whose text was generated by AI models at the author’s direction; consistent with widespread practitioner lore; contradicted by no one; measured by no one. It is real evidence that people *feel* a release. It is no evidence at all that anything happens in the tissue. It is the anchor phenomenon of everything that follows.

## Two experiments that catch the loop in motion

The evidence that these spots are under ongoing neural control has existed for decades, largely unread. In 1993, Hubbard and Berkoff inserted fine needle electrodes into trapezius trigger points and, simultaneously, into adjacent non-tender fibers. They recorded sustained spontaneous electrical activity in a one-to-two-millimeter nidus of every trigger point, and none in the non-tender sites, with higher amplitude in tension-headache and fibromyalgia patients than in healthy subjects. The knot is not merely stiffer than its surroundings; it is a small island of maintained activity in muscle nominally at rest. The authors guessed that sympathetically driven muscle-spindle contractions were the source; later literature favors endplate potentials; the generator remains contested.

“None in the non-tender sites” needs a qualifier. Skeletal muscle fibers receive their nerve supply in a band called the motor endplate zone, and faint electrical activity there — endplate noise — is a known finding. In 2002 Simons, Hong and Simons located the endplate zone electrically in eleven muscles of ten subjects and needled three kinds of site. Endplate noise appeared at all eleven trigger-point sites; [it also appeared at four of eleven non-tender sites that lay in the endplate zone but outside any trigger point]{claim=VASO-C034}; and [it never appeared at taut-band sites outside the endplate zone]{claim=VASO-C035}. The authors’ own summary is that the signature is “characteristic of, but is not restricted to,” the trigger point. Put the two studies together and the honest statement of the electrical finding is that [trigger points carry a sustained electrical signature more often than non-tender sites in the same endplate zone, and never where there is no endplate zone at all]{claim=VASO-C002} — a prevalence gradient, eleven of eleven against four of eleven against none, rather than an exclusive island. Hubbard and Berkoff’s silent control sites may simply have lain off the endplate zone. The Simons study was small, nonrandomized and unblinded, and its authors are the construct’s leading proponents; the finding nonetheless cuts against exclusivity, and it says something about where the signature lives: in the endplate zone first, and at the trigger point second.

The follow-up to Hubbard and Berkoff, from McNulty, Gevirtz, Hubbard and Berkoff in 1994, is the remarkable one. With electrodes in place in fourteen subjects, they administered mental arithmetic. [Activity at the trigger point rose; control sites in the same muscle stayed comparatively quiet; the subjects were not tensing]{claim=VASO-C003}. A purely mental event, involving no movement, turned up the signal inside one tender point and not a centimeter away. The brain has the knot’s address. Both studies are small, old, from one lineage, and never replicated with modern instrumentation; neither took any vascular measurement; and — the Simons result again — neither placed its control needle in a matched endplate-zone site, so whether the stressor selected the trigger point or simply any endplate zone is open. The essay this case grew from adds two follow-ups from the same lineage — relaxation training lowering the activity, and an infusion of the alpha-blocker phentolamine quieting the site — and candidate papers for both have been located but not retrieved; until one is, the autonomic-maintenance argument rests on stress induction alone.

Then, in August 2026, a study in *Nature Human Behaviour* supplied the regulatory counterpart. Mizrachi, Rottem and Rozenkrantz induced identical histamine skin-prick inflammation in the same fifty-seven volunteers on different occasions, in preregistered experiments, manipulating only where attention went. [Attending to the inflamed site produced roughly 1.5-fold smaller and faster-resolving wheal-and-flare responses in about ninety percent of participants across two cohorts — with no difference in skin conductance, heart rate, skin temperature or self-reported anxiety, and heart-rate variability higher under inward attention]{claim=VASO-C006}. A local anesthetic dissected two routes: a sensory one that lidocaine degraded and a top-down vagal one that survived it. What this shows is that cognition can write to a peripheral vascular bed at a chosen site without arousal. What it does not show is anything about knots, smooth muscle, or seconds: the timescale was tens of minutes and the route is vagal immune regulation, in a tissue the authors note the parasympathetic system does not directly innervate. It is an existence proof for a channel, not for the featured mechanism.

## The ratchet in the vessel walls

{plate:IMG-VASO-P02}

The body contains a second muscular system under no direct voluntary command: smooth muscle, lining the blood vessels, gut and airways, answering to autonomic state. Smooth muscle has a property skeletal muscle lacks, textbook physiology since Hai and Murphy formalized it in 1988: [the latch-bridge state, in which its molecular motors grip and then lock, holding tension at a small fraction of the usual energetic cost after the activating signal has faded]{claim=VASO-C010}. In the model, cross-bridges that have been switched off chemically — dephosphorylated — remain attached and detach only slowly, so a vessel can sustain high stress at low levels of activation. Arteries must hold tone for a lifetime; the latch is how they afford it. It is a kinetic trap, not damage — latched tissue looks normal under a microscope. And it is history-dependent: the tissue’s present state depends on what was done to it. A cheap, history-dependent hold that persists after its input fades is, in engineering terms, a memory element. Two questions follow. Is anything ever written to it? And does it exist in the vessels a knot would need?

Here the speed of the felt release becomes the crucial clue. Structural change in tissue — remodeling, scarring — takes days to weeks. [A change that completes in seconds, mid-exhale, must be a change of maintained state, not of structure]{claim=VASO-C011}: something the body is doing and can stop doing. Scar tissue does not release on an exhale. The inference is sound, and this case grades it as provisionally supported on physiological priors rather than on any record in its ledger — with two caveats. Its premise, that the felt release corresponds to an objective local event, is precisely the thing never measured. The one imaged change in a trigger point the ledger holds is from the Ballyns study: three active points followed after dry needling shrank on sonoelastography and their pulsatility index fell over subsequent visits — which shows the measures can move, over days, after a needle, and nothing about seconds or breath. And “state” is a bigger tent than “vascular”: sustained motor guarding is a state; so is fascial densification — the proposal, from fascia researchers, that viscous hyaluronan between fascial layers thickens and then thins again under pressure, movement and warmth. If densification can reverse in seconds, the knot could be a state without being a latch. Nobody in this ledger has yet retrieved the timescale, which is why the research agenda asks for it.

## What the arteriole record actually says

This is where the case’s own study lands, and it lands against the comfortable assumption. A frozen-criteria evidence map (study VASO-S001) asked a narrow question: where, by vessel type and caliber, has the latch actually been demonstrated with a contemporaneous readout of activation or energetic cost? Sixteen eligible rows, 1981 to 2022, answered three ways.

First, the energetic argument — that a knot could be held for almost nothing — rests entirely on large conduit arteries. Every measurement of oxygen consumption, lactate release or ATP turnover during maintained force comes from swine or porcine carotid preparations held at zero transmural pressure. No arteriole or resistance microvessel of any bed has ever had its holding cost measured. Searches aimed specifically at arteriole energetics returned nothing.

Second, the compartment the hypothesis names has been examined, and what was found does not look like a latch. Three rows are pressurized rat skeletal-muscle arterioles — cremaster and gracilis, roughly a hundred micrometers across — in which myosin light-chain phosphorylation, the molecular marker of activation, was measured against diameter. In all three, maintained constriction came with maintained or *rising* phosphorylation: 27.7 percent at 30 mmHg rising to 39.6 percent at 120 mmHg in one study; about 40 percent at 10 mmHg rising to about 55 percent at 80 mmHg in another, attributed there to calcium sensitization and actin polymerization. A 2000 paper states flatly that arteriolar tone “represents a state of maintained smooth muscle activation that requires increases in [Ca2+]i and myosin light-chain phosphorylation.” That is the opposite signature to the economical, dephosphorylated hold a latch requires. The cautions are real: none of the three was designed as a latch test; all held their stimulus present throughout, and myogenic tone is by construction a response to a maintained stimulus, so they could not have seen input-free persistence even if it exists; and the rows were built from abstracts. But the assumption that the arteriole was simply unexamined is gone.

Third, latch behavior is not generic across vascular smooth muscle. The one published comparison between a vessel and its own downstream branch — rabbit femoral artery against its saphenous branch — found sustained stress at falling calcium in the parent (42 percent phosphorylation) and a forty-percent stress loss in the branch (28 percent), attributed to motor-protein isoforms that do not support latch-bridge formation. One laboratory, one pair of papers, and nobody has followed the comparison further downstream. Vessel type and motor-protein phenotype are load-bearing variables, not incidental ones.

So the mechanism the knot hypothesis borrows is real where it has been studied, and unobserved — arguably pointed away from — where the hypothesis needs it. That is not a refutation. It is a mismatch, and a specific gap the research agenda now targets.

## What if blood talks back?

In 2008 the neuroscientists Christopher Moore and Rosa Cao proposed the hemo-neural hypothesis: that coupling between neurons and blood runs both ways — that [local vascular and hemodynamic state can modulate what nearby neurons do]{claim=VASO-C012}, through mechanical, thermal and chemical channels. It was a hypothesis paper; it demonstrated nothing new. Sixteen years later, in 2024, Jammal Salameh and colleagues reported in *Science* that physiological blood-pressure pulsations modulate central neuronal activity through mechanosensitive ion channels, in rat preparations and awake animals, on rapid timescales. The read path has a demonstrated mechanism. It is a mechanism of *instantaneous* modulation, in rat brain: it shows vessels can nudge neurons now, not that vessels can store anything and read it back later. Proponents argue that nothing in the logic is brain-specific and that peripheral sensory endings sit alongside the very vessels whose caliber they would sense. That extension is argument, not yet measurement.

## The synthesis, and what it would explain

The researcher Michael Edward Johnson has assembled these pieces into a program he calls vasocomputation, stated in three hypotheses of ascending ambition: that rhythmic vessel contraction acts as a compression sweep collapsing ambiguous neural patterns; that a vascular contraction freezes local neural patterns for its duration, functioning as a prediction and a medium-term memory; and that a contraction held long enough engages the latch and durably freezes nearby circuitry until the prediction resolves. Write, store, read: [vascular tension as a memory medium participating in mental life — with the grasping Buddhism calls tanha as its felt signature]{claim=VASO-C021}. The program is self-published, not peer-reviewed, and as of 2026 its experiments seek evidence rather than report it. The critical report commissioned for this case adds the sharpest objection: biological memory requires a state that depends on prior input, can later be read out, and discriminates between different prior inputs. A thermostat has hysteresis; it does not have an autobiography. The latch literature addresses none of these criteria, and the report notes that the nearest genuine write–store–read loop in a living flow network is a slime mold storing nutrient locations in the diameters of its own tubes — an organism very unlike us.

Whatever the fate of that grand identification, consider what the stack offers the humble knot. [A knot becomes a latched arteriole throttling its own neighborhood — chronic local ischemia at near-zero energetic cost, producing the acidic, sensitized milieu the microdialysis found, wrapped in secondary skeletal-muscle guarding]{claim=VASO-C020}. This would patch the oldest hole in trigger-point theory: the classic “energy crisis” model needed muscle fibers in permanent maximal contraction, a metabolic bonfire no one could account for, where a latch holds for almost nothing. It would explain why knots feel like autonomous objects, why they persist for years, why the Doppler findings show flow behaving as if something upstream were clenched — remembering that the authors of the Doppler study list muscle contracture compressing the bed as one candidate cause, and never mention smooth-muscle latch. And it would explain the two-key protocol. Smooth muscle takes no voluntary commands, but it answers to autonomic state, and [slow breathing with extended exhalation reproducibly shifts autonomic balance toward the parasympathetic]{claim=VASO-C013} — a 2018 systematic review documents the rise in heart-rate variability and respiratory sinus arrhythmia across studies of healthy people. Pressure perturbs the local loop; breath shifts the chemistry that governs unlatching. The roller is the read head; the exhale is the write head. Note, though, what the breathing evidence establishes: a global shift, measured on the heart, in people with no tender point in the study. The local, site-specific unlatching the hypothesis adds on top has never been measured.

## The conventional account, taken seriously

Every one of those explananda has a soberer candidate, and honesty requires displaying it at full strength. Tender points may be neuromuscular guarding: sustained low-level motor drive and endplate activity in skeletal muscle, centrally maintained and stress-sensitive. The EMG chatter is, by every published interpretation, skeletal-muscle electrophysiology — and the Simons finding places it in the endplate zone generally, at higher prevalence where the tissue is tender, which is what stress-sensitive endplates would produce without any vascular element. The chemical milieu may come from compression under guarding rather than from a throttled arteriole. The abnormal Doppler waveforms near trigger points are, by the imaging authors’ own account, as compatible with contracture squeezing the capillary bed as with anything constricting upstream — and one of the two resistance indices shows no difference at all. The felt release may be expectation and attention doing what they demonstrably do, riding the genuine but global parasympathetic shift of slow breathing, with pressure altering local sensation. Any rapid mechanical change may be fascial densification thinning rather than a vessel unlatching. And the construct itself has poor examiner reliability and no validated objective marker, so part of the observation base may be an artifact of training and expectation. This account needs no new physiology, which is its strength, and the only direct arteriole measurements available fit it better than they fit a latch. Its gap is the set of localized objective findings — a graded stiff region that blinded sonographers can measure, electrical activity that a mental task selectively turns up at one point and not a centimeter away, abnormal local chemistry and flow — that a purely central or interpretive story must still explain.

## The oldest anatomy text

{plate:IMG-VASO-P01}

Essentially every contemplative tradition that mapped the inner body arrived at the same three claims: there are knots, breath is the tool, and untying them changes consciousness. Tibetan tantric physiology describes channel-knots — rtsa mdud — constricting the flow of wind, untied by breath practice; Hindu yoga names the granthis; Chinese medicine records ashi points, tender spots named for the patient’s cry. The standard modern move is to file this as metaphor. The alternative reading is that [practitioners with extraordinarily trained interoception were producing first-person cartography of the vascular-autonomic tension system]{claim=VASO-C022} — channels as vasculature, winds as autonomic state, knots as latches. Proponents find it suggestive that the traditional maps cluster the important knots along the torso’s midline. But suggestive is all it is. This ledger holds no evidence record on the claim in either direction. Nobody has coded the traditional locations under blinded rules and tested the alignment against chance, and until someone does, every convergence is vulnerable to post-hoc matching — and even a genuine alignment with vascular geography would not show that anything latches. The traditions also preserved a warning, which this case records without adopting a mechanism: releasing held material faster than the system can integrate is destabilizing.

## The crux, and what would change our mind

Strip everything away and the disagreement is narrower than either camp admits. Both sides accept the latch as physiology. Both accept that slow breathing shifts autonomic state globally. Both accept that people feel releases, and that palpated points are measurably stiffer. The dispute funnels into one empirical question: when a knot “releases” on a slow exhale, does anything objective happen locally — a stiffness drop, a perfusion rise, time-locked to the breath, exceeding what pressure alone, expectation, and generalized relaxation produce?

What would move this case toward the featured hypothesis:

- Time-resolved imaging of a felt release showing stiffness falling and perfusion rising together within seconds of the exhale, at palpated sites but not sham sites, with the latch-specific ordering — blood first, stiffness second.
- A pressurized skeletal-muscle arteriole holding constriction after its stimulus is withdrawn, with falling phosphorylation and measured low energetic cost — the latch, in the vessel the knot needs.
- A retrieved primary study showing sympathetic blockade quiets the electrical nidus.
- A repeat of the mental-arithmetic experiment in which the trigger point rises and a matched endplate-zone control site in the same muscle does not.
- In an animal, different induced vascular states producing reliably different later neural responses under identical stimulation, with oxygenation clamped.

What would move it toward the conventional account:

- Felt releases without reproducible local transitions, or equal transitions at sham sites and under pressure alone.
- Fascial densification reversing in seconds under pressure with no perfusion change — a fast, non-vascular state.
- A matched endplate-zone control site rising as much as the trigger point under mental arithmetic — the signature relocated from the knot to stress-sensitive endplates generally.
- A paired-caliber study finding the non-latching motor-protein phenotype throughout skeletal-muscle arterioles.
- A knot census with pain-free controls finding that Doppler measures do not pick out the palpated spots.

## Where the ledger stands

The verdict is *unresolved*, and that is a finding rather than a shrug. The ladder is inverted: the best-evidenced rungs — the latch exists, slow breathing shifts the autonomic system, vessels can nudge neurons, palpated points are stiffer — are the least *diagnostic*, meaning they are exactly what conventional physiology predicts too and so decide nothing between the accounts. The rungs that would decide the case — that a release is objective, that the releasing element is vascular smooth muscle — are the ones with no evidence located, in either direction. The claim most exposed is the knot-as-latched-arteriole attribution, because the arteriole record leans against it and the vascular footprint at real trigger points is partial. The observation that has shifted most is the electrical nidus: still real, still stress-reactive, but now read as more common at trigger points rather than exclusive to them, and living in the endplate zone. The claim the whole case hangs from is the felt release, which is credible as an experience and worthless, on its own, as a mechanism.

The strongest argument for the hypothesis that this verdict does not answer is worth stating plainly. The classic energy-crisis account of trigger points has never explained how a fiber stays maximally contracted for years without exhausting itself; a latch would. The electrical signature is millimeter-scale and stress-reactive while surrounding muscle stays quiet, which is odd for diffuse guarding even if the signature also appears at a minority of other endplate-zone sites. Attention has now been shown to regulate a peripheral vascular bed at a chosen site without arousal. Every arteriole study that found maintained activation kept its stimulus on, so none could have seen a state that persists after input stops — the very thing a knot would be. And the hypothesis makes a timing prediction no rival makes — perfusion changes before stiffness — which is falsifiable and cheap. None of this is evidence that knots are latches. It is a reason the experiment is worth running.

## The research agenda

That experiment — ultrafast elastography and sensitive Doppler over a palpated knot, sites fixed in advance by blinded examiners, calibrated pressure through an instrumented probe, factorial controls, a button press at each felt release, and a mental-arithmetic block to catch stiffening during a purely cognitive event — would cost less than a mid-size grant and has never been run. It leads a program of twelve items, ranked by how much each would decide. Behind it: a paired-caliber study following the latch from a feeding artery down through successive arteriole orders, with a stimulus-withdrawal phase, in the compartment the knot needs. Then two cheap items that sharpen what the ledger already holds. The first is a retrieval task: six papers have been located but not opened, among them a 2025 elastography study of calf trigger points in runners reported to show most palpated points undetectable by palpation and imaging within minutes of pressure alone, with no breath instruction, and absent a day later — if it says what it is reported to say, it would be the first objective imaged record of a fast release, and it would qualify the two-key framing, since pressure alone sufficed; the same batch holds the relaxation and alpha-blockade papers behind the essay’s autonomic-maintenance argument. Nothing from any of them carries weight until it is read. The second is a small lab study: repeat the mental-arithmetic experiment with the endplate zone located electrically first and the control needle placed in a non-tender endplate-zone site, so that the localization argument for an addressable nidus is tested rather than assumed. Then the densification timescale; the phentolamine search; the fibromyalgia-era community surveys as a proto-census; the census nobody has taken — there is no graph of knot burden against age, anywhere, for something millions of people can find in thirty seconds — with pain-free controls, children and long-term meditators as the discriminating populations; a factorial trial separating the probe from the permission; the animal experiment separating vascular memory from vascular plumbing; the blinded coding of the contemplative maps; and the evidence map of the latch, already executed and reported above. A full-body ultrasound scanner announced in 2026 makes whole-body coverage imaginable, but it is a prototype built for body composition, not for the stiffness and flow channels a census needs, and it has no diagnostic clearance.

The machines exist. The practitioners exist. The experiments are small and specified. Someone should count. Either way, the knots are there. Press into one, and breathe out slowly.

assessment.synthesis: The ledger's ladder is inverted: the mechanism rung — latch physiology (VASO-E003), the slow-breathing autonomic shift (VASO-E009), vascular-to-neural mechanosensation in rat brain (VASO-E005) — is better evidenced than either the observations beneath it or the attributions above it, and every one of those records is credible without being diagnostic, because conventional physiology predicts each of them too. The observation base is now anchored in two primaries. Ballyns 2011 gives the stiffness component of VASO-C005 its first blinded-sonographer support (VASO-E023: graded stiff area 0.57/0.36/0.17 cm², AUC 0.9) and a group-level Doppler difference (VASO-E022), but the same source shows the vascular signature is partial — retrograde flow at 31% of palpably normal sites, a null resistivity index, a pulsatility index that cannot classify sites, no pain-free controls, and vessels of conduit caliber 1–2 cm from the point (VASO-E024, VASO-E025, VASO-E026), with the authors themselves listing contracture compression as a co-equal cause of the flow pattern (VASO-E027, which the ledger's second reader rightly notes reads as qualification rather than support). Simons 2002 (VASO-E031, VASO-E032) turns the electrical nidus from an exclusive island into a prevalence gradient that tracks the endplate zone first, which lowers the diagnosticity of VASO-C002 and exposes the control-site problem in VASO-C003. The anchor observation, a seconds-scale release on an exhale (VASO-C004), is supported only by proponent testimony (VASO-E014); the only imaged change in a trigger point is over visits after needling (VASO-E030). Where the thesis needs the latch, the record points the other way: pressurized skeletal-muscle arterioles show maintained or rising phosphorylation (VASO-E020), no arteriole energetic measurement exists (VASO-E019), and latch behaviour vanished one branch order downstream in the only paired comparison (VASO-E021). The memory attribution (VASO-C021) fails the write–store–read test (VASO-E017); the contemplative attribution (VASO-C022) has no record at all. Sensitivity: no single removal flips the case verdict, because each direction lacks decisive evidence independently. The record whose removal would most change the shape of the case remains VASO-E020 — without it VASO-C020 reverts from 'examined in its named compartment and mismatched' to merely 'untested'. VASO-E016 remains the single most important undermining record; VASO-E031 is the record that most changed the reading of the observations, moving the nidus from an addressable element toward a property of the endplate zone. Unresolved is a finding, not a default: the decisive experiment (VASO-R001) is specified, cheap and unrun, and both outcomes remain live.
assessment.steelman: The classic energy-crisis account of trigger points has never explained how a skeletal-muscle fiber could remain near-maximally contracted for years without exhausting itself, and the latch is the one known physiological device that holds tension for almost nothing — the puzzle the conventional account cannot dissolve is exactly the puzzle a latch would. The electrical signature is confined to one to two millimeters and is selectively turned up by mental arithmetic while surrounding muscle stays quiet; that it also appears at four of eleven other endplate-zone sites does not explain why it is present at eleven of eleven trigger points, nor why a stressor picks the tender one. Blinded sonographers find a graded stiff region at exactly the sites examiners palpate, and the arteries nearby behave differently — the footprint a throttled bed would leave, whatever else could leave it. Voluntary attention has now been shown, in preregistered human experiments, to regulate a peripheral vascular bed at a chosen site with no change in arousal — the write channel the synthesis needs, demonstrated. Every arteriole study reporting maintained activation held its stimulus present throughout, so none could have detected a state that persists after input stops, which is the only state a knot requires; and the latch-competent versus latch-incompetent motor-protein phenotype has never been surveyed in skeletal-muscle arterioles under chronic sympathetic drive, the condition the hypothesis posits. Finally, the hypothesis makes a distinctive, falsifiable timing prediction that neither guarding nor densification makes — perfusion rises before stiffness falls — and it can be tested for the cost of a small grant. None of this shows that knots are latches; it is the best reason the assessment cannot yet be closed against them.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: Muscle knots are maintained vascular-autonomic states rather than structural lesions: microvascular smooth muscle held in the latch-bridge state, throttling local blood flow and sensitizing local nerve endings, with secondary skeletal-muscle guarding layered on top — writable by stress, readable as stiffness and ache, releasable by sustained pressure combined with slow exhalation. More broadly, vascular tension functions as a memory element participating in mental life, the physical implementation of what contemplative traditions call clinging, and the traditional anatomies of knots and channels are first-person maps of the same system.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not over whether people feel tender spots, not over whether palpated points are measurably stiffer, and not over whether smooth muscle can latch — all three are common ground. The crux is whether anything objective happens locally when a knot 'releases' on a slow exhale: does stiffness fall and perfusion rise within seconds, time-locked to the breath, beyond what pressure alone, expectation and generalized relaxation produce — and, if it does, is the releasing element vascular smooth muscle rather than skeletal-muscle guarding or fascial densification? Beneath that sit two further disputes. The latch has been demonstrated in large conduit arteries, and where pressurized skeletal-muscle arterioles have been measured they show maintained activation, not a latch signature. And the electrical signature that made the knot look like a discrete addressable element also appears at a minority of non-tender endplate-zone sites, so whether the brain addresses the knot or the endplate zone is open. Beneath all of it, the skeptical literature disputes whether the trigger point is reliably identifiable at all.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: A time-locked imaging experiment: ultrafast shear-wave elastography and sensitive microvascular Doppler over a palpated knot during breath-assisted release, with sites fixed in advance by blinded examiners, calibrated pressure through an instrumented probe, factorial controls (pressure with normal breathing, slow breathing without pressure, sham sites, failed attempts), a button press at each felt release, and a preregistered prediction that stiffness drops and perfusion rises together within seconds of the exhale, exceeding all controls, with perfusion leading stiffness. Felt releases without reproducible local transitions, or equal transitions at shams, would return the knot to the guarding-and-interpretation account. Companion studies decide the mechanism and the localization: a paired-caliber, pressurized arteriole preparation with a stimulus-withdrawal phase testing whether latch capacity persists into skeletal-muscle arterioles; a repeat of the mental-arithmetic experiment with a matched endplate-zone control site; a retrieved densification timescale telling the keystone experiment whether a stiffness drop without perfusion change is a live alternative; and a Doppler census with pain-free controls, since every existing flow comparison sits inside symptomatic muscle.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Tenderness and its relief need no vascular memory. Tender points are neuromuscular guarding — sustained low-level motor drive and endplate activity in skeletal muscle, centrally maintained and stress-sensitive — possibly with altered fascial gliding from hyaluronan densification between fascial layers. The electrical signature is endplate noise, a property of the endplate zone that is more prevalent where tissue is tender; a stressor that raises sympathetic drive to endplates would raise it. The acidic, mediator-rich milieu follows from compression under guarding as readily as from a throttled arteriole, and the high-resistance Doppler waveforms near trigger points are, by the imaging authors' own account, as compatible with contracture squeezing the capillary bed as with distal constriction — while a second resistance index shows no difference at all. The felt release is expectation and attention doing what they demonstrably do, riding the genuine but global parasympathetic shift of slow breathing, with pressure altering local sensation; any rapid mechanical change is densification thinning or guarding switching off, not a vessel unlatching. Nothing is stored locally: the brain stops guarding, regionally or globally, and interpretation supplies the rest. A stricter version adds that manual trigger-point identification has poor examiner reliability and no validated reference standard, so part of the observation base may be an artifact of training and expectation. This account requires no new physiology, and the only direct arteriole measurements available fit it better than they fit a latch. Its gap is the set of localized objective findings — a graded stiff region that blinded sonographers can measure, spontaneous electrical activity that a mental task selectively raises at one point, abnormal local chemistry and flow — that a purely central or interpretive story must still account for.

components.label: The phenomenon at the fingertip: tender points exist and differ instrumentally (VASO-C001, C005, C030, C031–C033, C036)
components.note: Blinded sonoelastography separates active, latent and normal sites in a graded way and local arteries differ on one Doppler index at group level; but a second index is null, retrograde flow appears at 31% of normal sites, there are no pain-free controls, palpation is the unreliable reference standard, and the biochemical elevation was not purely local.

components.label: The neural signature: a stress-reactive electrical nidus (VASO-C002, C003, C034, C035)
components.note: Real and stress-reactive, but a prevalence gradient across the endplate zone rather than an exclusive island; the control sites in both lineage studies may have lain off the endplate zone, and the recorded activity is skeletal-muscle electrophysiology with no vascular measurement.

components.label: The autonomic lever: breath and attention reach the periphery (VASO-C013, C006)
components.note: Slow breathing reproducibly shifts autonomic balance globally, and voluntary attention regulates a peripheral vascular bed at a chosen site without arousal over tens of minutes; neither record concerns tender points, smooth muscle, or seconds.

components.label: The latch and its reach into the compartment the knot needs (VASO-C010, C011)
components.note: Latch-bridge physiology is established in conduit arteries; no arteriole energetic measurement exists, pressurized skeletal-muscle arterioles show maintained activation rather than a latch signature, and latch behaviour vanished one branch order downstream in the only paired comparison. The state-not-structure inference is sound but unanchored to any measured release.

components.label: The hemo-neural read path (VASO-C012)
components.note: Blood-pressure pulsations modulate neurons through mechanosensitive channels in rat brain — instantaneous modulation, not storage, and not the human periphery.

components.label: The attributions: knots as latched arterioles, vascular tension as memory, contemplative maps as cartography (VASO-C020, C021, C022)
components.note: No direct evidence located in either direction for the two linchpins; the memory claim fails the write–store–read test; the contemplative claim has no evidence record at all. The arteriole record leans against C020 without refuting it.

researchPriority.reason: The decisive experiment (VASO-R001) is specified, costs less than a mid-size grant, has never been run, and either outcome is informative: a positive result would open a new mechanism in musculoskeletal medicine and a negative one would return a widely practiced release protocol to the guarding-and-interpretation account. Several cheap desk and small-lab items (VASO-R012, VASO-R011, VASO-R008) would materially sharpen featured claims within weeks.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The only records are the originator's own statement of the program (VASO-E013, context, self-published, no experimental validation) and the critical report's argument that hysteresis is not memory (VASO-E017): biological memory requires input-dependent state, later readout, and discrimination between prior inputs, none of which the latch literature addresses. The read path exists as instantaneous modulation (VASO-E005) and a write channel exists at the scale of minutes (VASO-E008), but no record shows vascular state storing anything and reading it back. Nothing contradicts the claim either; it is untested rather than disconfirmed.

treatment.plainLanguage: The idea that the tension in your blood vessels is part of how you think and hold expectations — that clinging has a physical location in vessel walls.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: No evidence record tests it, so it cannot presently move the case in either direction; if the animal experiment (VASO-R005) showed vascular state biasing later neural responses with oxygenation clamped, it would become the most diagnostic claim in the ledger.
treatment.strongestObjection: A latch is a kinetic trap with hysteresis, like a thermostat; nothing shows it stores content-specific information that can be read out later, and the only living flow network shown to do so is a slime mold whose tubes are its own body.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An animal preparation in which different induced vascular states produce reliably different later neural response distributions under identical stimulation, with metabolic variables clamped.
A clean negative in the same design, showing vascular manipulation affects neural gain only through instantaneous perfusion — which would collapse the claim to ordinary neurovascular physiology.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The critical report's audit finds no direct evidence for either linchpin — objective seconds-scale release, or vascular smooth muscle as the releasing element (VASO-E016, strong undermining). The case's own evidence map adds that no arteriole energetic measurement exists (VASO-E019), that pressurized skeletal-muscle arterioles show maintained or rising phosphorylation rather than a latch signature (VASO-E020), and that latch behaviour vanished one branch order downstream in the only paired comparison (VASO-E021). Ballyns 2011 (VASO-E027) records high-resistance flow near trigger points, which the claim predicts, but the authors name contracture compression, inflammation and transducer pressure as co-equal causes and the vessels are conduit-scale; it adds nothing that separates the accounts. The originator's statement (VASO-E013) is context. The verdict is unresolved with the lean against; 'contradicted' would overread studies that never withdrew their stimulus.

treatment.plainLanguage: A knot is a small blood vessel's muscle stuck in its low-energy lock, starving the tissue around it, with ordinary muscle tensing on top — not injured or scarred tissue.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the case's central attribution; demonstrating a smooth-muscle latch at a tender point, or a perfusion-first release signature, would decide the thesis against guarding and densification, and excluding it would collapse the featured hypothesis to the conventional account.
treatment.strongestObjection: Where the arteriole has actually been measured with the right molecular readout, maintained constriction comes with maintained activation, not an economical dephosphorylated hold; the mechanism is borrowed from conduit arteries and has never been observed in the tissue it is supposed to explain.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Time-resolved elastography and Doppler showing perfusion rising before stiffness falls at palpated sites, not shams, within seconds of an exhale.
A pressurized skeletal-muscle arteriole holding constriction after stimulus withdrawal with falling phosphorylation and measured low energetic cost.
A paired-caliber study finding the non-latching motor-protein phenotype throughout skeletal-muscle arterioles, or fascial densification shown to reverse in seconds without perfusion change.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record in the ledger bears on this claim in either direction. The proposed alignment of traditional knot locations with vascular or autonomic anatomy has never been coded under blinded rules or tested against chance, so every reported convergence is vulnerable to post-hoc matching.

treatment.plainLanguage: The claim that Tibetan, Indian and Chinese maps of body knots and channels are accurate first-person records of the same vessel-and-nerve tension system, made by people with highly trained inner sensing.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even a genuine above-chance alignment of traditional knot locations with vascular geography would not show that anything latches or stores; it would show the maps are empirical documents about tenderness and anatomy, which the conventional account can absorb.
treatment.strongestObjection: Human anatomy offers many salient landmarks — joints, nerve plexuses, dense fascia, arterial branch points — so any set of points chosen for tenderness will 'align' with something; without preregistered coding there is no test.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Preregistered anatomical coding of the rtsa mdud, granthi and ashi-point corpora showing alignment with vascular branch points or sympathetic chains better than chance under blinded rules.
The same coding showing alignment no better than with a null set of anatomical landmarks, which would retire the convergence argument.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Hai and Murphy's latch-bridge model (VASO-E003, strong) reproduces the textbook observation of high sustained stress at low myosin phosphorylation in smooth-muscle preparations. The evidence map qualifies its scope (VASO-E021): latch behaviour was present in a rabbit femoral artery and absent in its own saphenous branch, so the capability is real but not generic across vascular smooth muscle, and nobody has followed the comparison into arterioles.

treatment.plainLanguage: The muscle in blood-vessel walls can lock into a low-energy grip and keep holding after the signal that told it to contract has gone.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Conventional physiology predicts this too; the latch's existence in arteries decides nothing about knots unless it is shown in skeletal-muscle microvessels under stimulus withdrawal.
treatment.strongestObjection: The one vessel-versus-branch comparison found latch behaviour vanishing one branch order downstream, attributed to motor-protein isoforms, so the capability cannot be assumed in the resistance vessels a knot would need.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A paired-caliber study showing latch capacity persisting into skeletal-muscle arterioles would raise the claim's reach; the same study showing the non-latching phenotype throughout would confine the claim to conduit arteries.
Independent replication or refutation of the femoral–saphenous divergence.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record supports the inference directly; the grade rests on the physiological prior that tissue remodeling takes days to weeks, so a change completing in seconds must be a change of maintained state. The only imaged change in a trigger point the ledger holds (VASO-E030, context) is over visits after dry needling in three cases — it shows the measures move, not that they move in seconds. The premise, that a felt release corresponds to an objective local event, is untested (VASO-E016).

treatment.plainLanguage: If a knot really does let go in a few seconds, it must be something the body was actively doing, not damaged tissue — scar does not release on an exhale.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Decides state versus structure but not vascular versus guarding versus densification: sustained motor guarding and fascial hyaluronan thinning are both states, so a fast objective release would engage this claim without favoring the latch.
treatment.strongestObjection: The conditional has never been triggered — no time-resolved measurement shows a tender point objectively releasing in seconds — and 'state' includes several non-vascular candidates.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Time-resolved imaging showing a stiffness or perfusion transition within seconds of a felt release, which would satisfy the antecedent.

Retrieval of the reported 2025 runners' elastography study (VASO-R012) showing palpated points undetectable minutes after pressure alone — a first objective fast-release record, though at minutes rather than seconds.
A densification timescale in seconds, which would keep the claim true while removing the vascular reading's exclusivity.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Moore and Cao's 2008 paper states the hypothesis without demonstrating it (VASO-E004, context). Jammal Salameh and colleagues (VASO-E005, strong) show blood-pressure pulsations modulating central neuronal activity through mechanosensitive ion channels in rat preparations and awake animals — a demonstrated mechanism for the vascular-to-neural direction, but instantaneous modulation in brain, not storage and not the human periphery.

treatment.plainLanguage: Blood flow and vessel pressure can change what nearby nerve cells do, not just feed them.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Fast mechanosensitive modulation is compatible with every account of knots; it becomes diagnostic only if vascular state is shown to carry a trace that biases later neural responses (VASO-R005).
treatment.strongestObjection: The demonstration is of moment-to-moment modulation in rat brain; the extension to peripheral sensory endings and to stored content is argument, not measurement.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Demonstration of mechanosensitive vascular-to-neural modulation in peripheral sensory ganglia or muscle afferents.
An animal experiment showing induced vascular states bias later neural responses under identical stimulation, or its clean negative.

claimAssessments.reasoning: A systematic review of slow-breathing studies in healthy humans (VASO-E009, strong) finds reproducible increases in heart-rate variability and respiratory sinus arrhythmia consistent with a shift toward parasympathetic dominance. The measurements are global cardiovascular indices; no local tissue or tender-point endpoint exists.

treatment.plainLanguage: Breathing slowly, especially with long exhales, reliably calms the body's automatic nervous system.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Both accounts predict the global shift; the local, site-specific unlatching the hypothesis adds on top has never been measured.
treatment.strongestObjection: A heart-measured global shift in people with no tender point in the study says nothing about what happens at a knot.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A factorial trial (VASO-R003) showing breath adds a local effect at knots beyond rolling alone and beyond generalized relaxation — or showing it adds nothing local.

claimAssessments.reasoning: A systematic review of examination-reliability studies (VASO-E011, strong) concludes manual trigger-point examination has not been shown reliable or valid and lacks an accepted reference standard; the Quintner–Bove–Cohen critique (VASO-E010, moderate) argues the construct is circular, and drew a rebuttal. Proponents concede the point in their own discussion section (VASO-E029, weak): palpation remains the reference standard and is subjective.

treatment.plainLanguage: Experts cannot reliably agree where a trigger point is, there is no gold-standard test for one, and researchers argue about whether the concept is sound.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It softens the observation base for every account and forces any decisive experiment to solve blinded, instrumented localization first; it does not itself favor guarding over latch, since a vascular mechanism is compatible with the critics' 'it isn't the muscle' instinct.
treatment.strongestObjection: The review assesses manual examination, not instrumented detection; blinded sonoelastography now separates palpated site classes with AUC 0.9, so imaging-anchored localization may escape the problem.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A validated instrumented reference standard with demonstrated inter-examiner reliability, which would retire the claim's force.
A knot census in which instrumented measures fail to pick out palpated spots, which would strengthen it.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Support is weak and second-hand: proponent testimony (VASO-E015), an introduction citing a 1986 clinic-based prevalence estimate for a pain syndrome rather than a count of tender points (VASO-E028), and a feasibility note on a scanner (VASO-E018, context). The critical report qualifies the claim (VASO-E012): the reproducibility and ontological status of the discrete palpable spot are themselves disputed. The community tender-point surveys the essay cites have not been retrieved. The shared experience is vast; the instrumented population record is nearly empty.

treatment.plainLanguage: Most people have small, very sore spots they can find in their own muscles.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Common ground between accounts; its distribution across age and body, if ever measured, would constrain mechanisms but the bare existence claim decides nothing.
treatment.strongestObjection: No census exists; the only population figures are second-hand and concern a pain syndrome, and the discreteness and palpability of the spots are contested in the reliability literature.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Retrieval of primary population tender-point-count surveys (VASO-R010) reporting distributions by sex, age and distress.
A blinded, instrumented knot census (VASO-R002) with pain-free controls.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Hubbard and Berkoff (VASO-E001, moderate) found sustained spontaneous activity in a 1–2 mm nidus of every trapezius trigger point and none in adjacent non-tender fibers. Simons, Hong and Simons (VASO-E031, moderate, qualifying) found endplate noise at 11/11 trigger-point sites, 4/11 non-tender endplate-zone sites, and 0/11 taut-band sites off the endplate zone, concluding the signature is characteristic of but not restricted to the trigger point. The claim as stated — more prevalent at trigger points than at endplate-zone controls, absent off-zone — is what both records together support. Both studies are small, old, from proponent lineages, and the Simons design was unblinded; neither measured vasculature.

treatment.plainLanguage: Needle recordings find ongoing electrical chatter at trigger points more often than at nearby non-tender spots in the same nerve-supply band, and never where there is no such band.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A sustained, localized electrical signature is what a purely interpretive account must still explain; but its tracking of the endplate zone fits the conventional skeletal-endplate reading at least as well as an autonomically maintained element, and nothing in it is vascular.
treatment.strongestObjection: The signature lives in the endplate zone first and at the trigger point second — the silent controls in the 1993 study may simply have been off the zone — and by every published interpretation it is skeletal-muscle electrophysiology.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A retrieved primary showing sympathetic blockade quiets the nidus (VASO-R009/R012), which would strengthen autonomic maintenance without making it vascular.
Modern needle EMG with matched endplate-zone controls (VASO-R011) showing either a sharp trigger-point excess or none.

claimAssessments.reasoning: One study of fourteen subjects (VASO-E002, moderate) found mental arithmetic raised trigger-point EMG while control sites in the same muscle stayed comparatively quiet, without generalized tensing. It is the same lineage as VASO-E001, never replicated with modern instrumentation, and took no vascular measurement. Simons 2002 (VASO-E031) shows endplate noise occurs at non-tender endplate-zone sites, so the control sites may not have been matched for endplate-zone position — the selectivity may be for the endplate zone rather than the knot. Candidate follow-up papers on relaxation and alpha-blockade have been located but not retrieved.

treatment.plainLanguage: Giving someone a math test makes the electrical chatter at one of their trigger points rise, while nearby muscle stays quiet — a purely mental event reaching one spot.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Stress-reactivity of a millimeter-scale site is awkward for diffuse guarding and natural for an addressable maintained element, but sympathetic drive to endplates or spindles fits the data without any vascular storage, and the control-site design cannot exclude a zone-wide effect.
treatment.strongestObjection: The control needle may have sat off the endplate zone, so the study may have compared an active endplate zone with electrically silent tissue rather than a knot with a matched control.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A repeat with electrically located endplate zone and a matched non-tender endplate-zone control under mental arithmetic (VASO-R011): selective rise at the trigger point would restore the addressable-nidus reading; a comparable rise at the control would relocate the phenomenon.
Retrieval of the relaxation and phentolamine papers (VASO-R012) showing bidirectional autonomic modulation.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The sole record is first-person testimony from the hypothesis's proponent (VASO-E014, weak), consistent with practitioner lore, contradicted by no one, measured by no one; the critical report's audit finds no synchronized time-resolved imaging of any release (VASO-E016). The claim concerns a felt release and is credible as an experience report; nothing in the ledger shows an objective local event. A located-but-unretrieved 2025 study is reported to show objective disappearance of palpated points under pressure alone, without breath, which if confirmed would qualify the two-key framing.

treatment.plainLanguage: Press steadily on a sore knot and breathe out slowly, and within seconds it can feel like it lets go.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: As testimony it decides nothing: expectation, attention and the global relaxation of slow breathing predict a felt release without any local event. It would become highly diagnostic only once measured — a time-locked local transition exceeding controls would engage the state-not-structure argument.
treatment.strongestObjection: A felt release is exactly what attention and expectation produce, and the one objective fast-release study located so far reportedly needed no breath at all.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The keystone experiment (VASO-R001) showing stiffness and perfusion transitions time-locked to the exhale at palpated but not sham sites.
Felt releases with no reproducible local transition, or equal transitions under pressure alone, which would return the phenomenon to interpretation plus global relaxation.
Retrieval of the 2025 runners' elastography study (VASO-R012) and what it says about pressure alone.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Biochemistry: microdialysis in about nine volunteers found an acidic, mediator-rich milieu at active points, elevated remotely too (VASO-E006). Stiffness: blinded vibration sonoelastography in 44 patients separates active, latent and normal sites in a graded way with AUC 0.9 (VASO-E023, moderate) — the claim's strongest component. Blood flow: pulsatility index higher and retrograde flow more frequent near active sites at group level (VASO-E022), but the resistivity index is null, the pulsatility index cannot classify sites, and blood-flow measures 'did not perform well as classifiers' (VASO-E024, VASO-E025); all comparisons sit within symptomatic muscle with no pain-free controls (VASO-E026). The 2021 imaging review (VASO-E007) is characterized only second-hand. Sites were selected by palpation and both primaries share one NIH lineage.

treatment.plainLanguage: Places examiners call trigger points really are measurably different — more acidic and inflamed, stiffer on ultrasound, with somewhat different blood flow in nearby arteries — though the blood-flow difference is partial.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Every measured difference is compatible with guarding: contracture compresses vessels and produces an acidic milieu, and the Doppler authors name compression as a co-equal cause. The differences are what the conventional account must explain, not what decides against it.
treatment.strongestObjection: The vascular signature is a gradient across symptomatic muscle rather than a marker — 31% of palpably normal sites share the waveform, one resistance index shows nothing, and the vessels are conduit-scale, 1–2 cm from the point.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A Doppler and elastography census with pain-free controls (VASO-R002) showing whether the flow abnormalities track palpated points at all.
Microvascular perfusion measured in the muscle bed itself at trigger points versus matched controls.
Retrieval of the Zhang 2009 skin blood-flow study (VASO-R012) adding or failing to add an autonomic-vascular abnormality at latent points.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Preregistered within-subject experiments in 57 volunteers (VASO-E008, strong) found attending to a histamine skin prick produced ~1.5-fold smaller and faster-resolving responses in ~90% of participants across two cohorts, with no difference in skin conductance, heart rate, skin temperature or anxiety and higher heart-rate variability; lidocaine dissected a sensory route from a surviving vagal route. Single lab, very recent, acute healthy-skin model, mediators not directly measured. The grade is held below well_supported for want of independent replication.

treatment.plainLanguage: Simply paying attention to an inflamed spot on your skin makes the swelling smaller and shorter-lived, without any sign of stress change.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: An existence proof that cognition can regulate a peripheral vascular bed at a chosen site without arousal — the write channel the synthesis needs — but the route is vagal immune regulation over tens of minutes in skin, which every account can accept; it says nothing about knots, smooth muscle or seconds.
treatment.strongestObjection: The authors note the parasympathetic system does not directly innervate skin and the timescale is minutes, so the demonstrated channel is not the seconds-scale local unlatching the hypothesis requires.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent replication in another laboratory.
An analogous attention manipulation at a tender point with local stiffness and perfusion endpoints.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Ballyns 2011 (VASO-E022, moderate) reports a median pulsatility index of 8.3 near active sites versus 3.0 near normal sites (P < .05) in 44 patients, with sonographers blinded to site class. The comparison is within symptomatic patients with no pain-free control group (VASO-E026), the index varied too widely to classify individual sites, and the vessels are pulsatile arteries or enlarged arterioles >1 mm, 1–2 cm from the point.

treatment.plainLanguage: In patients with neck pain, arteries near their active trigger points show a sharper, more resistive pulse than arteries near normal-feeling spots in the same muscle.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Increased downstream resistance is what a throttled bed would show, but the authors name muscle contracture compressing the capillary bed, inflammation and transducer pressure as equally plausible causes; nothing separates arteriolar smooth muscle from mechanical compression.
treatment.strongestObjection: Large variance, no pain-free controls, and conduit-scale vessels a centimeter or more from the point; the index is a group-level difference in symptomatic muscle, not a signature of a knot.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Replication with a pain-free control group and microvascular perfusion in the muscle bed itself.
A time-resolved change in the index during a felt release, which would connect it to the anchor phenomenon.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Ballyns 2011 (VASO-E022, moderate) reports retrograde diastolic flow at 15 of 49 (31%) palpably normal sites, against 55% of active and 40% of latent sites. Because all patients had trigger points elsewhere in the muscle and there was no pain-free group (VASO-E026), the 31% may be a true baseline rate or spillover from neighbouring points; the source cannot say which.

treatment.plainLanguage: Nearly a third of the normal-feeling spots in these patients' muscles showed the same backward blood flow between heartbeats that was read as abnormal at trigger points.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It cuts against the vascular footprint as a marker of a discrete knot: the waveform is a gradient across symptomatic muscle, which fits regional guarding or regional sympathetic tone at least as well as a latched arteriole at the palpated spot.
treatment.strongestObjection: The 'normal' sites sat five centimeters from trigger points in symptomatic muscle, so the finding may reflect spread of a real local abnormality rather than a baseline rate.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Doppler in pain-free controls showing a much lower baseline rate of retrograde flow, which would restore the finding as a marker of symptomatic muscle.
A comparable rate in pain-free muscle, which would remove the waveform as evidence of anything.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Ballyns 2011 (VASO-E023, moderate) reports stiff areas of 0.57 ± 0.20, 0.36 ± 0.16 and 0.17 ± 0.22 cm² at active, latent and normal sites (P < .01), with ROC AUC 0.9, 0.8 and 0.8, and sonographers blinded to clinical status. Single vibration frequency, shear elasticity not measured, sites selected by palpation, one NIH lineage.

treatment.plainLanguage: On ultrasound that shakes the tissue and watches where it fails to move, painful trigger points are the biggest stiff patches, tender-only ones smaller, and normal-feeling spots smallest.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The strongest instrumented evidence that palpated points are objectively distinct and graded, but it says nothing about what the stiff tissue is — contracted fiber, guarding, fascial change or vascular — so it constrains no mechanism.
treatment.strongestObjection: Sites were chosen by palpation, so the contrast presupposes the classification it validates, and a single off-the-shelf vibration frequency was used without confirming frequency-independence.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Shear-wave elastography with quantified elasticity at blinded, prospectively fixed sites.
Time-resolved stiffness during a felt release, which would connect the stiff region to the anchor phenomenon.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Simons, Hong and Simons 2002 (VASO-E032, moderate) found endplate noise at endplate-zone sites outside trigger points in 4 of 11 muscles (P = 0.024 versus 11/11 at trigger points), with the endplate zone located electrically. Abstract only; 10 subjects; described by the source as nonrandomized and unblinded; authors are proponents of the construct.

treatment.plainLanguage: The electrical chatter taken as the trigger point's signature also shows up, less often, at non-tender spots in the same nerve-supply band.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It removes exclusivity from the electrical nidus and relocates the signature to the endplate zone first — the conventional skeletal-endplate reading — while leaving the prevalence excess at trigger points to be explained.
treatment.strongestObjection: Four of eleven is still far below eleven of eleven, so the finding qualifies rather than dissolves the trigger-point excess; and the study is small and unblinded.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Modern blinded needle EMG with matched endplate-zone controls (VASO-R011) reporting the prevalence and amplitude at each site class.
A stressor paradigm showing the excess vanishes or persists when controls are zone-matched.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Simons, Hong and Simons 2002 (VASO-E032, moderate) found no endplate noise at taut-band sites outside the endplate zone in any of 11 muscles (P = 0.000034). Same limitations as VASO-C034: abstract only, small, unblinded, proponent authors.

treatment.plainLanguage: Where a tight band of muscle lies outside the nerve-supply zone, the electrical chatter does not appear at all.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It ties the electrical signature to skeletal-muscle endplates rather than to tightness as such, consistent with the conventional reading; it does not speak to vasculature in either direction.
treatment.strongestObjection: A null in eleven muscles of ten subjects is a modest sample, and taut bands off the endplate zone may be a different phenomenon from the tender nidus.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A larger blinded needle study reporting activity at off-zone taut bands.
Any demonstration of a non-endplate generator at tender sites.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Ballyns 2011 (VASO-E024, moderate) reports no differences in resistivity index between normal, latent and active sites, and that the pulsatility index was not a good classifier because of large variance. Within-patient comparison in symptomatic subjects; the authors attribute the similarity partly to proximity of normal sites to trigger points.

treatment.plainLanguage: One of the two standard ultrasound measures of downstream blood-flow resistance shows no difference at all between trigger points and normal spots.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A null on one index makes the vascular signature partial rather than categorical; it weighs modestly against a strong local vascular abnormality, but the proximity of 'normal' sites to trigger points could mask a real difference.
treatment.strongestObjection: Because all sites sat in symptomatic muscle a few centimeters apart, a regional vascular abnormality would produce exactly this null while still being real.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Resistivity index in pain-free controls differing from symptomatic muscle, which would reinterpret the null as regional spread.
Microvascular perfusion in the muscle bed itself showing or failing to show a local deficit.
